TESTIMONY OF
Deirdre Gilbert
Department of Marine Resources
The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying
Neither for nor Against
LD 1279 An Act to Require the Department of Marine Resources to
Conduct Biotoxin Testing of Cultured Scallops
(Sponsor's Amendment) Before the Committee on Marine Resources
Sponsored by Representative Eaton
Date of Hearing: May 1, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine
Resources, my name is Deirdre Gilbert, Director of State Marine Policy for the Department of Marine Resources, and I am testifying on behalf of the Department neither for nor against LD 1279 (as
amended by the sponsor).
Maine's Marine Biotoxin Monitoring Program is administered by the Department's Bureau of Public Health. lt uses the standards outlined in the National Shellfish Sanitation Program (NSSP) to monitor levels of Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning (PSP) and other marine biotoxins in the shellfish of the State of Maine.
When toxin is found at levels near or above where human illness may occur, closures to the harvest of shellfish areas are implemented. Maine has historically had high levels of PSP, more commonly known as "Red Tide" , during the warmer periods ofthe year. In 2008, and twice in 2009, several Maine
citizens were hospitalized for PSP toxicity after harvesting shellfish from areas closed for PSP. To
prevent illnesses and possible deaths, shellfish samples are collected by DMR statewide between
March and October and evaluated at certified laboratories. Data are then interpreted and appropriate
closures are made when necessary to protect public health.
All areas along the coast during any active bloom season require weekly monitoring at a minimum.
High risk areas and high risk species have additional considerations for management. DMR employs a
regional management strategy closing mussels, European oysters, surf clams, razor clams, and carnivorous snails from May until the end of the bloom season. Lease-specific exception areas to the regional and emergency closures for aquaculture lease sites (standard and experimental) require
industry to submit a signed Memorandum Of Understanding (MOU) to DMR to establish testing
requirements. if the aquaculture lease holder wants or requires the services of private lab testing an
additional private lab MOU must also be signed and submitted to DMR.
Certain species (i.e. whole or roe-on Atlantic scallop, whole or roe-on bay scallop, surf/hen clams, Arctic surf clams, and razor clams) pose an additional biotoxin risk because they are slow to eliminate toxins (domoic acid and saxitoxin) due to their capacity to store these toxins within their tissues. in
addition, some of these species can also transform less toxic compounds into more toxic compounds

within their bodies. Because high risk areas are prone to chronic exposure to toxin (annual bloom events) and higher toxicities than other areas, high risk species grown in these areas require testing year-round even when phytoplankton blooms are no longer in the water. Scallop adductor muscles do not accumulate toxin and are exempt from biotoxin testing requirements as long as adductor muscles
are the sole product.
Requirements for biotoxin testing of high risk species through the MOU process include:
0 Annual DMR biotoxin MOU signed by lease holder and DMR v Annual private lab MOU signed by lease holder, private lab, and DMR
0 Written notification 30 days prior to initial harvest
0 Collection and provision of samples according to DMR sampling protocols and chain of custody requirements, with results provided to DMR directly from private lab
0 Results from three samples each seven days apart to initiate harvest
Q Written permission provided by DMR to allow initial harvest 0 Sampling thereafter in consultation with DMR and at established frequencies
LD 1279 would establish a new pilot program, in which biotoxin testing of whole or roe-on scallops
would be treated differently than other high risk species in that transportation and testing of samples
would be at the Department's expense, rather than the lease holder. All of the MOU requirements
would still apply. Because the Department cannot do the work associated with the transportation and testing within existing resources, in the amendment provided by Representative Eaton there is a $50,000 general fund appropriation. These funds would cover a Department contract to provide for the transportation of samples, and extraction of samples as well as consumable lab supplies. However, because this appropriation was not included in the Governor's Budget, the Department is testifying neither for nor against the amended bill.
As a point of clarification, the amendment also specifies that the Department is not required to provide
testing for scallops grown on limited-purpose lease sites. We believe that the intent here was to
exclude product grown on limited-purpose aquaculture (LPA) license sites, which are not leases. There
is a current prohibition on biotoxin monitoring through the MOU process for LPA sites.
Thank you for your consideration, and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
10047788:
Testimony in support of LD 1279, An Act to Support the Growth of Maine's Farmed Atlantic Sea Scallop Industry Through Funding Biotoxin Testing and Other Services.
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler and members of the Marine Resources Committee, my name is Don Hudson, retired President of Chewonki in Wiscasset, and a resident of Arrowsic. I have actively supported the establishment of a farmed sea scallop industry in Maine since participating in a Maine delegation visit to the Japanese prefecture of Aomori in October 2010. Fishermen and scientists in Aomori established a first-in-the-world farmed sea scallop industry in 1963, and members of our delegation were very interested to learn more about how this robust industry had grown. A visit by a Maine delegation in the late 1990s had resulted in an effort by Maine lobstermen and Maine Sea Grant Extension scientists to learn how to collect early growth stage scallops called spat. A nascent sea scallop aquaculture industry was poised to take off in Maine.
As a result of our visit, seeds were planted in Maine and Aomori to move from concepts and plans to pilot projects. The owner of an Aomori-based manufacturing company, Hiroaki Sugiyama of Mutzu Kaden, joined delegations visiting Maine from Aomori in 2012 and 2013. As the chair of the Maine Aomori Sister State Advisory Council, I had the opportunity to help keep some attention on the dream of growing scallops in Maine for commercial markets. As our relationship with Sugiyama-san strengthened, in October 2016, Hugh Cowperthwaite of CEI, Dana Morse of Maine Sea Grant Extension, and I led a delegation of Maine lobster fishermen and marine scientists to take a deep dive into scallop aquaculture as it is practiced in Aomori, Japan.
Suffice it to say, our visit in 2016 has resulted in the launch of a commercial Atlantic sea scallop industry in Maine, and LD 1279 is an important next step to ensure its long-term success. Significant private investments have been made to facilitate the transfer of technology from Aomori and Hokkaid, and Maine fishermen have been nimble in adapting methods and techniques designed for Japanese waters to the different conditions found here on the coast of Maine.
The 2-year pilot project to include cultured scallops and scallop roe in the Marine Shellfish Toxins Monitoring Program at the Department of Marine Resources will provide commercial scallop growers with the same level of rigorous testing that assures the public that scalloped shellfish are safe to eat. When we visited Aomori in 2016 there was no commercial sea scallop aquaculture in Maine. Now, Maine Department of Marine Resources recorded $1 million in landings in 2024.
Atlantic sea scallop aquaculture is poised to take off in Maine and I believe that it has earned the right to be included in a monitoring and testing program that is aimed, in part, to facilitate the sale of shellfish in the marketplace.

Hugh Cowperthwaite, Senior Program Director, Fisheries & Aquaculture Program
CEI, Brunswick, Maine HughCowperthwaite@ceimaine.org
Dear Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler and Members of the Marine Resources Committee:
My name is Hugh Cowperthwaite,,l am a resident of Falmouth, and I am hereto speak in favor of LD 1279 to
support the growth of Maine's Farmed Atlantic Sea Scallop Industry. Today I represent Coastal Enterprises,
Inc. (CEI) where I am Senior Program Director for CEl's Fisheries and Aquaculture Program. In this role I am
always on the lookout for opportunities for diversifying Maine's fisheries.
I first learned about Maine's relationship with Aomori, Japan when I was invited to participate in a delegation to visit Aomori in October 2010. Our goal was to learn about Aomori's energy practices and fisheries and share
our experiences from Maine. I spent the next several days learning about Aomori's robust commercial scallop farming industry centered around Mutsu Bay. I had never seen anything like it. The people, their kindness,

My mind was racing, and I said to myself "we can do this in Maine" . I made friends quickly with ourlapanese

Farmed scallops are a shining example of a truly sustainable fishery and the opportunity to build this industry is here in front of you all today. I urge your support with this modest request to create a pilot program under the direction of the Department of Marine Resources to help facilitate a biotoxin testing program that includes covering the testing costs of farmed sea scallops grown on lease sites.

10047091:
Marnie Crowell Sunset LD 1279
In favor of Farmed scallop Biotoxin Testing bill, LD 1279
I am a natural history writer with a Master of Science degree in Biology, a long-time resident on Deer Isle. For a number of years I have worked with Marsden Brewer, a well known pioneer in farming sea scallops. My husband Ken is a now-retired ecologist whose research was on the islands off Stonington. We have watched Marsden and his son Bob closely for some years, going out with them on their boat, visiting their shop, and enjoying their scallops. In every way we came to see farming of sea scallops as highly beneficial to the health of Penobscot Bay, potentially a good boost for coast economies, and delicious for the table.
It is clear that making trips to take sea scallop specimens for expensive biotoxin testing is a major obstacle in both time and money. For other cultured species of shellfish in Maine (oysters, blue mussels) shellfish testing is conducted by the MDMR without a fee to the harvesters. I believe it's time to provide dedicated funding by State legislative mandate to help MDMR cover these costs and adopt a policy to treat farmed scallop testing costs similarly to those of other cultured shellfish.
When Marsden once said that people in this country do not know what to do with whole sea scallops, I took that as a challenge. Having traveled around the globe for ecological research, I had some insights into the ways whole scallops are cooked in other countries. Marsden supplied scallops and we cooked and tasted and tested and produced a number of easy and delicious recipes. Down East Books is now in the process of publishing our whole sea scallop cookbook.
As our public becomes more aware of what a treat whole sea scallops are -- checking all the right boxes -- more of Maine's mariners will be interested in farming sea scallops. It is clear that the current situation forcing sea scallop farmers to make long trips to take sea scallop specimens for expensive biotoxin testing is a major obstacle in both time and money.
The time is right for the legislature to do the right thing and pass LD 1279!
Marnie Reed Crowell Sunset, Maine 04684

10047584:
Phoebe Jekielek Rockland LD 1279
Letter to the Committee on Marine Resources - in Support of LD 1279, An Act to Support the Growth of Maine's Farmed Atlantic Sea Scallop Industry Through Funding Biotoxin Testing and Other Services.
Dear Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler and Members of the Marine Resources Committee:
My name is Phoebe Jekielek, I am a resident of Rockland, ME, and I am here to speak in favor of LD 1279 to support the growth of Maine's Farmed Atlantic Sea Scallop Industry. I have been working with both wild harvest and farmed scallop industries since 2013 and continue to conduct research on the biologies and ecologies of farmed and wild scallops. A toxin monitoring effort for cultured scallops will help decrease barriers to entry into this emerging industry by providing consistent and temporally and spatially diverse data on the retention of biotoxins in scallop tissues. The existing data on biotoxins is promising in that we may be able to identify certain times of year where biotoxin retention is most concerning, and can make regulations to accommodate that, but we need more consistent data and from beyond Penobscot Bay. More data is always better. There are many leases out there listing scallops as a species to grow, but very few are growing. Testing could increase the number of farms engaging in scallop aquaculture by informing a pathway to further establishing and growing a whole scallop market in Maine and beyond. This pilot project may also pave the way to developing processes and protocols for other potentially harvestable species that may require similar assessments as they expand. This program will decrease barriers to entry for interested parties as well as barriers to growth for existing farms. I had the delicious opportunity just a few weeks ago to gorge myself on some whole scallops raised on Marsden Brewer's farm and even cooked by the man himself. It was the best meal I've had this year so far, and I really like to eat! Again, I support LD1279 in the hopes of continued growth and success of the scallop aquaculture industry here in Maine. Please fund this pilot project for the following two years to collect essential data. Thank you very much for your time and have a great day!
Phoebe Jekielek Rockland, ME

Dear Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler and Members of the Marine Resources Committee:
My name is Togue Brawn, I'm a resident of Bath, Maine, and I work out of a seafood processing plant in Bremen, Maine. I'm asking you to support LD 1279 to support the growth of Maine's Farmed Atlantic Sea Scallop Industry.
I worked for the Maine Department of Marine Resources from 2007 to 2011, and in that time I helped craft regulations to make Maine's scallop fishery more sustainable. Restoring our scallop resource was important, because Maine's commercial fishing industry was (and is) dangerously reliant on one species: lobster. Diversification is, critically important to the long term viability our fishing communities. Scallops represent a fantastic opportunity, because although we currently produce only 2-3% of US sea scallops, they are vastly superior to the scallops produced by the much larger offshore fleet. Did you know that Maine's bays produce scallops with different flavor profiles? They are all delicious, and I'm proud to have helped make Maine's scallop fishery more sustainable.
We now have an opportunity to grow that industry even more. When I was at DMR, I wanted to try to find a way to support the harvest of whole scallops, or at the very least, scallops with the roe attached. But because resources were limited I was always told "There's absolutely no way that's going to happen, Togue." Well, in the years since I left DMR, it did happen. DMR, Sea Grant, CEI and of course Marsden Brewer have worked to show that it's possible to grow and consume whole scallops from Maine's inshore waters. Now that we know it can be done, the time has come to find resources to help grow the industry.
Whether it's lantern nets or lines or even the newly patented cages similar to lobster traps, scallop farming represents a fabulous opportunity for small boat fishermen to diversify their income stream. But it's not going to happen if fishermen have to bear the full cost of biotoxin monitoring. I truly believe Maine can become the Mecca of scallops. We will never compete with New Bedford when it comes to quantity. But we will beat them every time when it comes to quality. Maine is the only state capable of producing farmed sea scallops, and we need supply in order to build market. I hope you'll support this bill, and help find a way to fund it, because it would be a shame to miss this great opportunity.
Yours, truly,

Good afternoon, Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and honorable members of the Marine Resources Committee. My name is Virginia Olsen, I am a fisherman from Stonington, ME. I urge you to support LD 1279 An Act to Require the Department of Marine Resources to Conduct Biotoxin Testing of Cultured Scallops.
In the past, the department has offered a pay-to-test program- I don't think many folks used it. Why, you may ask, would I support it? We want to make sure we give our harvesters or growers every opportunity to participate in value-added products. Scallops are shelled at sea in Maine- the little orange and white roe is discarded with everything but the adductor muscle (what we eat). Roe is very popular with Michelin-star restaurants, wanting to elevate their customers' dining experience. Why are scallops considered a high risk? Scallops filter over a gallon of water an hour- if biotoxins are present in the water, then the scallop will concentrate those biotoxins, making whoever eats them very sick. With a good sampling protocol, Maine could be a leader in the high-end restaurant world. This is the definition of value-added products. The report back period should be long enough to see any trends that could raise concerns. I also think this should be opened up to any grower, or dealer of farm-raised scallops. I would be happy to answer any questions.
Thank you,
Virginia Olsen
